== Should cannabis be legalised? ==

{{Debate
|topic=Cannabis
|expanded-topic=the legalisation of cannabis
|progress=Constructed debate
|debate-warnings=Unbalanced debate
|introduction={{Subsection
|content='''Should cannabis be legalised?''' The debate brings together competing assessments of public health, individual liberty, public safety and the effects of prohibition. Supporters of legalisation emphasise product regulation and a smaller illicit market; opponents highlight the risks of normalisation, dependence and commercialisation.

This debate focuses on France. Experience elsewhere informs some of the arguments, but findings need to be understood in relation to the country, period and indicators studied.
}}{{Subsection
|title=Decriminalisation and legalisation: two different reforms
|content=In this debate, '''decriminalisation''' means removing or reducing criminal penalties for certain conduct. Depending on the approach adopted, administrative sanctions may remain. Under French law, reclassifying a ''délit'' as a ''contravention'' does not, by itself, take an offence outside the criminal law.

'''Legalisation''' permits previously prohibited activities within a defined framework, whether production, distribution, sale or use. It does not necessarily mean unrestricted or unregulated sales. Restrictions on age, advertising, quality and quantity may vary.

Portugal's reform, which came into force in 2001, decriminalised drug use, acquisition and possession for personal use under the conditions set out in the law. It did not legalise trafficking or establish a legal commercial drug market<ref>[https://www.euda.europa.eu/system/files/media/publications/documents/11331/portugal-cdr-2019.pdf EMCDDA, Portugal — Country Drug Report 2019, “National drug laws”].</ref>.
<references />
}}{{Subsection
|title=The legal position in France
|content=Unlawful use of controlled drugs remains a criminal offence in France. The Service Public information page reviewed on 21 August 2026 states that use carries a maximum penalty of one year's imprisonment and a €3,750 fine. Offences relating to supply, trafficking, cultivation or driving after drug use must be distinguished: this maximum cannot be applied indiscriminately to all of them<ref name="sp-usage-2026">[https://www.service-public.gouv.fr/particuliers/vosdroits/F33341?lang=en What is the risk for drug use?], Service Public / DILA, information page reviewed on 21 August 2026.</ref>.

'''A fixed fine does not mean decriminalisation of use'''

According to the same dated page, the fixed fine is €500, reduced to €400 if paid within fifteen days and increased to €1,000 after forty-five days. This procedure does not make drug use legal and is not the same as reclassifying the offence as a ''contravention''. The amounts and conditions must be checked against the law in force for the period concerned<ref name="sp-usage-2026" />.

<references />
}}{{Subsection
|title=Comparing experience in other countries
|content=Canada opened a legal market for non-medical cannabis in 2018. Its expert panel reported progress in 2024 in regulated supply and the shift in demand towards the legal market, alongside persistent problems, particularly protecting young people and addressing high-THC products<ref>[https://www.canada.ca/en/health-canada/services/publications/drugs-medication/legislative-review-cannabis-act-final-report-expert-panel.html Legislative Review of the Cannabis Act: Final Report of the Expert Panel], Health Canada, 2024.</ref>.

Portugal's approach is one of decriminalisation and should not be equated with this form of legalisation. In each country, rules on use, the organisation of supply, health indicators and the role of the illicit market need to be considered separately.
<references />
}}

== Drug dependence is not independent of the person and their environment. Drugs are a way of coping with life, not the cause of dependence ==

{{Argument
|quotes={{Quote
|quote=The question is this: does dependence on an illicit drug occur independently of the person and their environment? In that case, the drug causes the dependence. Or does dependence develop because the habit has met a person's needs in a particular environment? In that case, the drug is a solution, a way of coping with life, rather than a cause.
These apparently innocuous questions are fundamental when assessing whether prohibition makes sense. The belief that illicit drugs cause dependence independently of the relationship a person develops with them and the circumstances in which they are used is the public's primary justification for prohibition. If the answer is that drugs help some people cope with their lives, and that some of those people develop a harmful habit, addressing the cause of the problem does not mean banning drugs. Drugs were one means among others. Addressing the problem means helping the person and/or changing their living conditions.
If we had to ban every product or behaviour to which some people are vulnerable to harmful dependence, we would have to ban sweets, junk food, television, computer games and even work and romantic relationships.
|authors=Lise Beauchesne
|work=Les drogues. Les coûts cachés de la prohibition
|page=133-134
|publisher=Lanctôt
|date=2003
|warnings=AI-translated quote
}}
|sections=Philosophy, Health, Society
|keywords=cannabis, legalisation, decriminalisation, health, addiction, dependence
}}

== Cannabis legalisation in Canada works better than prohibition ==

{{Argument
|summary=Canada's state-regulated legalisation demonstrates that strict cannabis regulation works better than prohibition.

* '''Description:''' Full legalisation with strict regulation (minimum age, advertising restrictions, production controls and state distribution).
* '''Examples:''' Canada and some US states.
* '''Advantages:'''
** A substantial reduction in the black market.
** High tax revenues to fund public programmes.
** Control over product quality and the varieties available.
* '''Disadvantages:'''
** The need for substantial legislative and administrative infrastructure.
** Some consumers continue buying on the black market because legal prices are high.
* '''Results:'''
** '''Canada:''' A smaller black market and better product quality, although youth consumption remains a challenge.
** '''Overall assessment:''' The best model for a nationwide approach, but one that requires constant monitoring and adjustment.
|sections=Law, Economy, Politics, Health, Society
|keywords=black market, taxation, public health issues
|webliography={{Web reference

== Cannabis regulation in Uruguay works better than prohibition ==

{{Argument
|summary=Uruguay's state-regulated legalisation demonstrates that strict cannabis regulation works better than prohibition.

* '''Description:''' Legalisation with state control over production and distribution. Only residents may buy cannabis, and quantity limits apply.
* '''Advantages:'''
** Almost complete elimination of the black market.
** State control over quality and prices.
** Tax revenue to fund prevention programmes.
* '''Disadvantages:'''
** Heavy bureaucracy and restrictions that can put users off.
** Difficulty persuading consumers accustomed to the black market.
* '''Results:'''
** A substantial reduction in the black market, but a slight increase in overall consumption.
** '''Overall assessment:''' A viable model that works better than strict prohibition, with scope for adjustment.
|sections=Law, Economy, Politics, Health, Society
|keywords=black market, public health issues, taxation
}}

|quote=General population surveys provide another measure of availability by asking people how easy they think it would be, or actually is, to obtain cannabis. == Regulated distribution can place limits on commercial strategies ==

{{Argument
|quotes={{Quote
|quote=Prohibition laws have made the illicit drug trade a thriving international market.
These sellers operate in ways that meet the same needs as any legal market: identifying potential customers, ensuring repeat business, attracting new customers and so on. But since the trade, potency and quality of the products are unregulated, anything goes when it comes to expanding that market, whether selling drugs to children or introducing extremely toxic products. Some sellers aim to create lifelong customers by encouraging patterns of consumption more likely to cause dependence than other, safer ways of using drugs. Products also change over time to maintain customers' interest, creating trends and regularly bringing new products onto the market […]. Sellers also try to reach the widest possible customer base by offering drugs across a broad price range […]. Similarly, they seek to expand the market geographically by dumping drugs in previously little-affected areas to attract new customers. This situation should come as no surprise. The illicit drug market is a highly profitable global market. It is worth sellers' while to use the best possible techniques to distribute and promote their products.
|authors=Lise Beauchesne
|work=Les drogues. Les coûts cachés de la prohibition
|publisher=Lanctôt
|date=2003
|warnings=AI-translated quote
}}

|keywords=cannabis, legalisation, decriminalisation
